The popular narrative is that prompt engineering is a skill you learn, a set of techniques you apply, a craft you refine. And maybe it is, for people using ChatGPT for one-off questions. But in a sustained working relationship with a coding assistant, what actually happens is closer to what happens with any colleague: you develop shared context, and the shared context makes the communication shorter.

You install an AI coding assistant. You type a prompt. It writes some code. You fix the parts it got wrong. You type another prompt. This is the loop, and for most people it stays the loop forever. Prompt, generate, fix, repeat.

I did this for about three months. It was useful. I built things faster than I would have alone. I explored codebases I didn't know. I generated documentation nobody else was going to write. The tool was good at its job, and I was good at asking it to do that job, and that was the whole story.

Today, every question finds its way to your desk. The quote waiting on your approval. The crew schedule that changed again. The Friday report someone builds by hand. None of it is hard. It all just needs you.

Many business owners find that a wide range of questions and tasks end up on their desk. These can include quotes awaiting approval, schedule changes, and weekly reports that are compiled manually. While none of these tasks are particularly difficult, each of them requires the owner's involvement.

During a Walkthrough, the process is examined from start to finish with input from the team. Bottlenecks are identified and documented, and a report is delivered within three business days, including recommended next steps.

For busy business owners, it can be challenging to step back and identify what needs to change. That is why our process begins by talking with the people who do the work, rather than focusing on software.

For example, client onboarding may require numerous reminders, reporting may take an entire afternoon, or a process may only work when the owner is present to manage it. Typically, the only alternatives are to hire another coordinator, purchase another subscription, or work late. These options can be costly over time.

Is the goal to replace existing staff? No. The aim is to free up team members to focus on higher-value work. Approaches that involve monitoring employees or that are designed solely to reduce headcount fall outside the scope of this work.
